title: Overfitting and the bias-variance trade-off
summary: A flexible model can fit its training data perfectly and still fail on new data. Training error only falls as flexibility grows, while test error falls and then rises. Expected test error splits into bias squared, variance and irreducible noise.
llm_link: Language model training is monitored with the loss on held-out text: if the training loss keeps falling while the held-out loss rises, the model is memorising. Very large networks can also show double descent, where test error falls again past the point where the model can fit the training data exactly.
key_ideas: Underfitting: the model is too stiff to follow the pattern (high bias). Overfitting: it bends to fit the noise (high variance).
Training error never rises as flexibility grows; test error is U-shaped. The bottom of the U is the model you want.
Bias: error from systematic wrongness. Variance: how much the fitted model changes when you redraw the training data.
Expected squared test error = bias² + variance + noise. The noise is a floor no model can beat.
More data, a simpler model or regularisation lower variance; always judge on data the model has not seen.

quiz.q: As you raise the polynomial degree, why can the training error never go up?
options: Because higher degrees use less data
Because a higher-degree polynomial can always copy the lower-degree fit (set the extra coefficients to 0) and possibly do better
It can go up if the learning rate is wrong
quiz.explain: The degree-d polynomials include all lower-degree ones, so the best fit at degree d is at least as good on the same training points. Least squares finds that best fit exactly.

quiz.q: Predict the diagnosis: a model has training error 0.01 and test error 0.90.
quiz.explain: A tiny training error with a large test error means the model fitted details of the training set that do not carry over: overfitting.

quiz.q: A bathroom scale always reads 2 kg heavy. In bias-variance terms, its error is…
options: Bias: a systematic error that averaging many readings cannot remove
Noise: it can be learned away
quiz.explain: Bias is a consistent offset from the truth. Averaging many readings cancels random scatter (variance) but leaves bias untouched.

quiz.q: You collect five times as much training data for a degree-9 model. Which term of the error does this mainly shrink?
quiz.explain: More points pin the flexible curve down, so refitting on a fresh sample moves it much less. Bias (the model's built-in limits) and the noise floor do not change.

quiz.q: During language model training, the training loss keeps falling but the loss on held-out text starts rising. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is starting to memorise its training text
The held-out text is too long
quiz.explain: A widening gap between training and held-out loss is the classic sign of overfitting. Engineers watch it and keep the checkpoint with the best held-out loss.

problems.solution:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x_tr = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 1, 12))
y_tr = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x_tr) + rng.normal(0, 0.25, 12)
x_te = rng.uniform(0, 1, 200)
y_te = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x_te) + rng.normal(0, 0.25, 200)

def errors_by_degree(degrees):
    train_err, test_err = [], []
    for d in degrees:
        coefs = np.polyfit(x_tr, y_tr, d)
        train_err.append(np.mean((np.polyval(coefs, x_tr) - y_tr) ** 2))
        test_err.append(np.mean((np.polyval(coefs, x_te) - y_te) ** 2))
    return train_err, test_err

def best_degree(degrees):
    tr, te = errors_by_degree(degrees)
    return list(degrees)[int(np.argmin(te))]

problems.title: Measure variance directly
problems.prompt:
Variance is how much the fitted model moves when the training data is redrawn. Write predictions_at(x0, degree, n_trials): for each trial t, draw a fresh training set with make_data(seed=t), fit a polynomial of the given degree, and record its prediction at x0. Return the predictions as a NumPy array.

Then compare predictions_at(0.95, 1, 50).std() with predictions_at(0.95, 9, 50).std().

tests.name: one prediction per trial
tests.code:
p = predictions_at(0.5, 3, 20)
assert p.shape == (20,), f'expected 20 predictions, got shape {p.shape}'

tests.name: flexible models vary more
tests.code:
s1 = predictions_at(0.95, 1, 50).std(); s9 = predictions_at(0.95, 9, 50).std()
assert s9 > 3 * s1, f'degree 9 should scatter much more than degree 1 (std {s9:.3f} vs {s1:.3f}); make sure each trial uses make_data(seed=t)'

tests.name: uses different data each trial
tests.code:
p = predictions_at(0.5, 1, 5)
assert p.std() > 0, 'all predictions are identical: draw new data in every trial'

hints: x, y = make_data(seed=t); coefs = np.polyfit(x, y, degree)
